canberra.title: ACT Government to put updated public service offer to vote
canberra.snippet: The ACT Government has topped up its enterprise agreement offer to public servants with earlier, higher superannuation contributions and ...
canberra.content:
Public servants protest in May, promising more industrial action. Photo: Ian Bushnell.

The ACT Government has topped up its enterprise agreement offer to public servants with earlier, higher superannuation contributions and inflation-linked cost-of-living payments.

In an email to staff, Deputy Director-General, Office of Industrial Relations and Workforce Strategy, Robert Wright, said the government intended to put this new offer to a vote in August.

It comes after workers rejected the previous offer made in March and embarked on a campaign of protected industrial action.

The offer maintains a 9 per cent pay increase in equal instalments over three years, with a twice-yearly increase of 1.5 per cent in July and February.

But the government has acknowledged the risk that a 3 per cent annual pay increase may not keep pace with the cost of living and has included a $600 cost-of-living payment if the ACT’s annual CPI reaches 3.5 per cent or higher, increasing to $1000 if it reaches 4 per cent or higher.

“This strengthened offer is a response to the feedback that the government received from industrial partners throughout bargaining,” Mr Wright said.

As well, superannuation contributions will rise to 13 per cent from 1 January 2028, six months earlier than proposed.

All entitlements included in the previous offers of 9 December 2025 and 11 March 2026 will stay.

If staff agree, salary increases will be backdated to July 2026; the first pay increase of 1.5 per cent will be paid on payday 8 October 2026.

All entitlements included in the previous offers of 9 December 2025 and 11 March 2026 will stay, but some new or modified ones have been introduced.

The parental leave framework has been revised, with all new parental leave provisions applying from the commencement of the agreement, instead of 1 July 2027.

Changes include 18 weeks paid leave for non-birthing parents; expanded access to parental leave for both parents, with the option to take leave concurrently and flexibly within a 24‑month period; and removal of the 12‑month service requirement for permanent employees to access the new Parental Leave entitlement.

Other new entitlements proposed are:

  • Increasing the cap of personal leave without the need for evidence from 7 to 10 days.
  • Increasing rest relief from 8 hours plus travel to a minimum of 10 hours inclusive of travel time between shifts.
  • Strengthened provisions on workload management, safe staffing levels and classification reviews to better support employees in their roles.
  • Employees who are breastfeeding will continue to have access to one hour for breastfeeding or expressing milk, with the introduction of additional reasonable time provided, including when an employee cannot access appropriate facilities and they are required to travel from their workplace to feed their infant or to express their milk.
  • Introduction of a new clause addressing the use of artificial intelligence in the workplace.
  • New provisions enabling the cultural expertise of Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander employees to be recognised as equivalent to formal qualifications and relevant experience for accelerated increments.
  • The Attraction and Retention Incentives (ARIns) framework has been broadened to explicitly recognise Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander cultural expertise, acknowledging and remunerating the additional cultural knowledge and skills required for certain roles.

Staff will receive a copy of the proposed agreement on 12 August to assess ahead of the ballot, which will open on 26 August and conclude at 4 pm on 8 September.

The new agreement will come into effect seven days after approval from the Fair Work Commission.

CPSU Regional Secretary Maddy Northam said union members’ action had delivered real results, forcing the ACT Government to come back with a revised and improved offer.

“And now it’s up to our members who will have their say on whether they accept these proposed changes or go back to the table to fight for better pay and conditions,” she said.

A CPSU member poll is now live and will close at 2pm next Monday, 27 July.

Public Service Minister Rachel Stephen-Smith said the updated offer sought to recognise and reward hard-working staff, while balancing the challenging fiscal environment facing the Territory.

Ms Stephen-Smith said the package delivered a sustainable and competitive outcome for employees and the broader ACT community, while maintaining the ACT Public Service as one of the country’s highest-paid public sector workforces.

She said the potential cost-of-living payments recognised ongoing uncertainty in the global and national economy.

“The updated offer also provides increased parental leave entitlements from commencement of the agreement, confirms backpay to July 2026 and brings forward superannuation increases,” she said.

“It also maintains the broader improvements proposed in March, delivering a comprehensive package that strengthens staff entitlements.”

canberra.title: Motorcyclist allegedly found with headlamp, pliers, accused of injuring officers during arrest
canberra.snippet: An accused motorcycle-riding thief has been labelled the “luckiest person” after being granted bail. Macgregor man Rhys Haral...
canberra.content:
20 July 2026

Rhys Haralambos Gregoriou, 30, will next face court in August. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

An accused motorcycle-riding thief has been labelled the “luckiest person” after being granted bail.

Macgregor man Rhys Haralambos Gregoriou, 30, briefly faced court on Monday (20 July).

An ACT Policing spokesperson alleged that at about 2:50 am this morning, officers were patrolling the Narrabundah carpark when a KTM motorcycle entered the carpark.

Police approached the motorcycle and directed the rider to stop, before Gregoriou allegedly tried to accelerate away from police.

It’s alleged that he then resisted attempts to arrest him, causing what the police spokesperson described as “minor injuries” to two officers.

He was ultimately handcuffed before being placed under arrest.

When police carried out an alcohol screening test, Gregoriou allegedly showed a positive result.

Police found “numerous items associated with burglaries”, the spokesperson alleged, after they searched the man and his backpack.

In court, Magistrate James Stewart noted that Gregoriou allegedly had a drone, medical gloves, a black beanie, pliers, and other items on him at the time of his arrest.

The spokesperson also alleged that officers discovered the motorcycle was stolen.

The prosecution didn’t oppose Gregoriou’s bid for freedom.

When granting him bail, Magistrate Stewart warned Gregoriou to “keep [his] nose clean”.

“I think you’re the luckiest person on my list today,” he said of the successful outcome.

Gregoriou has been charged with failing to stop a motor vehicle for police, riding a motor vehicle without consent, attempting to resist a Territory official, going equipped for theft and driving a motor vehicle with alcohol in his breath.

He will next face court on 11 August. No pleas were entered.

canberra.title: Robodebt whistleblower tells Federal Court she was threatened
canberra.snippet: One of the Robodebt whistleblowers is suing the Federal Government, claiming her job was threatened before she gave evidence to the royal...
canberra.content:
Jeannie-Marie Blake giving evidence wo the Robodebt Royal Commission in February 2023. Image: Screenshot.

One of the Robodebt whistleblowers is suing the Federal Government, claiming her job was threatened before she gave evidence to the royal commission into the illegal debt recovery scheme.

Jeannie-Marie Blake was a frontline Services Australia employee when she blew the whistle on Robodebt when the program was first piloted.

She later gave important evidence to the royal commission and has since claimed the agency told her that her testimony “could cost you your job”.

She gave her evidence to the royal commission and also to a subsequent Senate inquiry into whistleblowing protections.

Ms Blake has now filed proceedings in the Federal Court, alleging her department made repeated threats against her before and after her royal commission appearance.

The Federal Government has filed its defence papers to the court, saying Ms Blake was not threatened at all.

Ms Blake’s statement of claim lodged before the court alleges Services Australia, as her employer, mistreated her over her Robodebt evidence and acted contrary to the general protections regime in the Fair Work Act 2009 (Cth).

Services Australia has denied the claim.

The proceedings were filed in the Federal Court, and an initial case management hearing was held last week before Justice James Stellios.

Ms Blake is represented by the Human Rights Law Centre’s Whistleblower Project, which is Australia’s only specialist legal service for whistleblowers.

The centre has briefed Michael Seck and Miles Foran of counsel.

The centre’s associate legal director Kieran Pender said the Whistleblower Project is proud to stand with Ms Blake in seeking accountability for her mistreatment.

“Robodebt caused so much harm to so many Australians, and it could have been prevented if whistleblowers like Ms Blake and many of her colleagues were listened to from the start,” he said.

“Public servants must be able to blow the whistle to royal commissions and inquiries without fear of retaliation.

“We have repeatedly called on the Albanese Government to enact stronger whistleblower protections, including for royal commission participants.”

Ms Blake says her treatment at the hands of her then public service bosses left her suicidal and battling with alcohol.

In her court documents, Ms Blake alleges that while she repeatedly raised the unfairness and harms of the Robodebt scheme being piloted, she was told to quit her job if she was not going to administer it.

In 2023, she told the agency that she intended to give voluntary evidence to the royal commission.

She claims her boss responded: “You better make sure you cross your T’s and dot your I’s because this could cost you your job if you’re not telling the truth.”

She claims she was also told: “The only people giving evidence are the people that have been subpoenaed. You should get legal advice before giving evidence.”

In her evidence given to the Senate Legal and Constitutional Affairs Committee on 13 August 2025, Ms Blake spoke of the trauma her whistleblowing caused her.

“For most of my career, I have worked for Services Australia. I was on the frontline of the implementation of what became known as Robodebt,” she told that inquiry.

“As I explained in my testimony to the Robodebt Royal Commission, involvement in Robodebt was a deeply traumatic experience.

“I tried, from the very beginning, when I was part of an initial Robodebt pilot, to blow the whistle on the scheme.

“I immediately saw Robodebt for what the royal commission eventually concluded it to be: unlawful and deeply unethical. I thought it should be stopped, to never proceed beyond the pilot.

“But when I and others raised concerns, we were met with a clear, stark message: resign, transfer or comply. The message was as blunt as that: shut up or leave.

“Our concerns were ignored. Instead, we received threatening communications. Performance targets, threats of underperformance notices and code of conduct breaches were used to suppress dissent. Daily emails reminded us that if we spoke to anyone outside our team about our work, we could face termination.

“There was no safe, independent mechanism for staff to report concerns without fear of reprisal.”

canberra.title: AI rules for government agencies to ensure humans are kept ‘in the loop’
canberra.snippet: All government departments will be subject to new rules over the use of artificial intelligence in their decision-making processes, follo...
canberra.content:
The Federal Government is moving to ensure that fairness and accountability are built into all public-sector AI decision-making. Photo: File

All government departments will be subject to new rules over the use of artificial intelligence in their decision-making processes, following the establishment of the Office of AI within the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet.

Anthony Albanese set up the office last week and announced plans for far-reaching standards for the embrace of AI across sectors in Australia.

This includes how agencies use technology for automated decision-making.

Ministers are this week already drawing up draft rules for their portfolios to feed into the umbrella Office of AI so a coordinated approach can be adopted.

These new rules are aimed at ensuring safety and fairness are built into how AI is used in decisions and service provision.

Transparency is also a priority to ensure accurate decisions and avoid a lack of accountability in the process.

Human override is to be built into all decision-making processes.

Assistant Technology Minister Andrew Charlton said on Monday (20 July) that the Federal Government would ensure humans are “in the loop” in the provision of government services as AI is further embraced across the public sector.

“When it comes to the use of automated decision-making, which is using technology in government services, the government’s priority is to make sure that we are fair, that we have humans in the loop, that we have transparency and accountability,” he said.

“We do not want to go back to the type of situation that we had in Robodebt.

“We think that these tools, if they have the right governance around them, the right transparency around them, the right oversight around them, humans in the loop, can improve services for citizens, make those services better, fairer, quicker.

“The Attorney-General [Michelle Rowland] has been doing a lot of work on this, and the purpose of that work is to give Australians confidence that, as these types of automated technologies are introduced into government, they will be delivering them benefits, not delivering them risks.”

In his recent announcement, the Prime Minister gave an example of AI being used to enhance government work.

“Last week, the Department of Employment and Workplace Relations published real-time, data-driven analysis of AI’s impact on the labour market,” Mr Albanese said.

“The first research of this kind by any government anywhere in the world.

“It found that while some roles are changing, graduate employment is high.”

But the PM warned that he wouldn’t allow an ad hoc approach to the technology.

He said the government would ensure the standards would provide not only the flexibility to keep pace with change, but also to “get out in front of it” and deal with issues in real time – “without the bureaucracy having to contemplate every modification”.

Duty of care and privacy factors will be built into the legislation, expected to be introduced next year following the Federal Government’s consultation with states and territories and other stakeholders.

Beyond accountability in Australian Public Service agencies, great responsibilities will be placed on tech giants opening data centres in Australia.

But the incoming standards will only apply to centres established after the new laws are set in place.

Mr Charlton noted that there were already more than 200 data centres in Australia, posing a challenge for government policy.

“Those data centres consume electricity equivalent to about 2 per cent of our energy grid and there are projections that could grow very rapidly over the next 10 years, potentially even triple over the next 10 years,” he said.

“The government has been very clear that we are implementing this world-first AI data centre standard, and that standard will make sure that local communities are supported.”

Deputy Opposition Liberal leader Jane Hume, however, said the government’s approach was lacking detail.

She also warned against over-regulating.

“Talking about regulating AI by introducing rules for data centres is a little bit like saying, ‘Well, I’ve regulated the fishing industry by setting up a licensing regime for building boats’,” Senator Hume said.

“There’s so much more to it than that.

“Over-regulating them could, in fact, be a problem because it’s not just about setting up certainty; it’s also about alternative opportunities.”

Industry Minister Tim Ayres has also flagged the government’s intention to tackle predatory pricing practices enabled by AI.

In particular, it plans to ban retail surveillance pricing, which sets different prices for individual consumers based on their behaviour (achieved by farming consumer data).

“That is, using artificial intelligence to provide for different prices to different customers, perhaps on the basis of their income or their wealth or their circumstances,” Senator Ayres said.

“The Assistant Minister for Productivity and Consumer Affairs [Andrew Leigh] is responsible for working through making sure that our legal framework and our regulators are up to the task of protecting consumers from that kind of practice.”

canberra.title: Driver accused of leading police on early morning chase to escape arrest
canberra.snippet: A Lyneham man has faced court after he allegedly ran red lights and drove on the wrong side of the road to escape from police on the week...
canberra.content:
20 July 2026

Police allege the Sunday morning (19 July) chase spanned several inner-north suburbs. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A Lyneham man has faced court after he allegedly ran red lights and drove on the wrong side of the road to escape from police on the weekend.

Byron Thomas Hancock, 39, briefly appeared in the ACT Magistrates Court on Monday (20 July), where he did not apply for bail in relation to the alleged offending, and it was formally refused.

At about 3:40 am yesterday (19 July), police were conducting patrols in Ngunnawal when they observed a vehicle displaying registration plates that had allegedly been reported stolen.

Police attempted to stop the vehicle. The driver allegedly failed to stop and continued driving through several suburbs across Canberra’s north.

“It is alleged the driver committed a range of traffic offences during the incident, including failing to stop for police, driving through red traffic lights and driving on the wrong side of the road,” the spokesperson alleged.

“During the incident, tyre deflation devices were successfully deployed, and police continued coordinated efforts to safely monitor and contain the vehicle.”

Police said the vehicle eventually travelled into the City area before coming to a stop near the Alinga Street and Northbourne Avenue intersection at about 4:15 am.

Officers then arrested the 39-year-old, the vehicle’s only occupant.

Hancock, who police say is subject to parole conditions, has been charged with aggravated dangerous driving and failing to appear before the Sentence Administration Board.

No pleas were entered.

australia.title: Mockbuster review – how to survive the nightmare of directing a terrible low-budget horror film
australia.snippet: Struggling to make it in Australia, aspiring director Anthony Frith cold-calls the team behind Sharknado and bites off more than he can c...
australia.content:
‘A bad movie is better than no movie” is the motto of this behind-the-scenes documentary, which charts director Anthony Frith’s quest to make his debut feature for ultra-schlock studio The Asylum; it doubles up as an affable salute to film-making savoir-faire.

Stuck making corporate videos to support his young family, Adelaide-based Frith is in danger of letting his artistic ambitions atrophy. So he opts for career shock therapy by cold-calling The Asylum (of Sharknado notoriety) in Burbank, California and proposing he oversee one of their straight-to-the-digital-cesspit features.

It turns out that if working for The Asylum were a film genre, it would be the against-all-odds suicide mission type of story. Frith is given six days to complete filming on a new version of The Land That Time Forgot, which will be the studio’s first movie shot in Australia. The budget is subatomic, there is no finished script when he signs the contract and he is told, only days before the shoot, to secure his own production team. Relying on this extreme frugality to ensure their profit margins, The Asylum executives laughingly dote on their directors with quasi-sadistic fondness. Frith might just make it through this, they say – if he doesn’t try to get “artistic”.

Any such notions quickly go out the window. Facing the schedule from hell, Frith canvasses survival advice from The Asylum veterans, such as actor Eric Roberts, and low-budget grafters including horror wonderkid Danny Philippou, who scoffs that Frith looks broken before he’s begun. On the executive side, there’s something almost refreshing in The Asylum’s cynicism – the studio’s credo is that the majority of viewers have no patience for arthouse complexity, so why should film-makers? As the LA movie ecosystem dries up, these survivalist cockroaches may well be the last outfit standing; movie-biz expediency in its most atavistic form, where “the genre is the star”.

Frith can be candid too: chivvied through by Brendan Petrizzo, a faintly unsettling in-house producer with a frosted fringe, the director reflects that he may have found his natural level. Maybe … or maybe not. Presumably too harassed by shooting his disasterpiece, he sometimes struggles to break down his experience into dramatically parsable portions for this making-of documentary, leaning on voiceover to tell the story. But, ironically, he succeeds in making quite a good film; a companionable reflection on artistic aspirations, compromise and on-set camaraderie, all – true to The Asylum’s spirit – in a solid 90 minutes.

australia.title: Israel criticises Labor’s draft Palestine policy in rare foreign intervention ahead of party conference
australia.snippet: Statement by Israeli embassy in Canberra challenges proposed positions on settler violence and annexation of Palestinian territory Get ou...
australia.content:
Israel has made an intervention into the Labor party’s internal processes, publicly criticising a draft policy platform that it claims risks blaming Israel for the Gaza conflict while giving “insufficient attention” to the role of Hamas.

The Israeli embassy in Canberra issued a four-page statement on Monday challenging the proposed positions on Palestine, Hamas and settler violence in the West Bank, due to be debated at this week’s Labor national conference.

“The Embassy of Israel notes these policy motions are still in draft form, and will continue to engage constructively with the Australian Labor Party through the usual diplomatic channels,” the statement read.

“However, the embassy respectfully submits that several elements of the draft platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party while giving insufficient attention to the decisions, conduct and continuing obligations of the Palestinian leadership and terrorist organisations such as Hamas.”

It is unusual for a foreign state to involve itself in a domestic internal political matter such as a party conference, further exposing the tension between Labor and the Israeli government.

The Labor platform is debated at each triennial national conference to settle the party’s positions on a wide range of issues, including Israel and Palestine.

The language in the 2026 draft platform relating to Israel and Palestine is substantially different to the 2023 iteration, reflecting shifts in government policy following Hamas’ 7 October attack and Israel’s war in Gaza.

The 2023 document contained just three lines on Israel and Palestine, all of which related to recognition of a Palestinian state – a policy the government formally adopted last August.

The draft platform to be debated this week in Adelaide goes much further, including motions to express Labor’s opposition to the annexation of Palestinian territory and to call for an end to settler violence and the occupation.

The Albanese government has been consistent in condemning settler violence in the West Bank, last month joining with other western nations to impose new sanctions on perpetrators.

In the media statement, the Israeli embassy said settler violence – which it described as a “reprehensible but marginal phenomenon” – was given “disproportionate attention”.

“Those seeking peace would be better served to focus its scrutiny on the terrorism experienced by both Jewish and Arab Israelis at the hands of terrorist groups such as Hamas,” it said.

The embassy also appears to have seized on shifts in language between the first draft of the 2026 platform and the one that will be debated this week.

For example, one of the lines that was included in the first iteration – “Hamas must disarm and can have no role in the State of Palestine” – was dropped from the final draft.

The final draft platform does, however, single out Hamas as a perpetrator of terrorism and violent extremism.

The embassy said all political parties should frame their policies “not around assigning blame, but around the conditions that history demonstrations are essential for lasting peace”.

“[Israel] remains committed to a future in which Israelis and Palestinians live alongside one another in peace and security,” it said. “That future, however, cannot be built through unilateral political declarations or international pressure directed at only one side.”

The minister for multicultural affairs, Anne Aly, appeared unfazed when asked about the embassy’s intervention.

“You know, they will do what they feel is right,” she told ABC Afternoon Briefing.

The language in the platform is set to be contested with Labor’s pro-Palestine and pro-Israel contingents likely to push for changes on the conference floor.

The foreign affairs minister, Penny Wong, declined to comment.

australia.title: Inquest begins into Jesse Deacon’s fatal shooting by police, three years after his death
australia.snippet: The 43-year-old Sydney man was fatally shot within a minute of police knocking on his door, court hears New South Wales police fatally sh...
australia.content:
New South Wales police fatally shot a man who was self-harming in a Sydney public housing estate within a minute of knocking on his door and after a Taser failed to deploy, a court has heard.

On Monday, the NSW coroner’s court began its long-awaited inquest into the death of 43-year-old Jesse Deacon, almost three years to the day since he was shot in Glebe on 19 July 2023.

The deputy state coroner David O’Neil heard that Deacon lived with treatment-resistant schizophrenia and fell into a group of about 30% of people with the illness for whom treatment is “incredibly complex”.

Since his death, Deacon’s mother, 82-year-old Judy Deacon, has become one of the state’s leading advocates calling for change in how police respond to mental health call-outs. She told the court she was foregoing legal aid and would represent herself, imploring that any recommendations from the inquest are listened to.

The counsel assisting the coroner, Donna Ward SC, walked through the chronology of police actions leading up to Deacon’s death. In her opening statement, Ward said three police officers responded to the welfare callout, which was described in their dispatch service as a self-harm incident involving “cut wrists”.

There was also a later warning that the person who lived at the address had HIV, which the court heard was incorrect, and could assault police “without provocation”.

Ward said that at at 11.56pm police knocked at Deacon’s door and said: “Hello mate, just the police, can you open the door please.”

At 11.57pm the officers kicked open the door, and then Deacon came out with a “large knife in hand” and an officer deployed a Taser, which failed. Less than a second later another officer fatally shot him.

Ward told the court the police’s system did not include warnings about his mental health challenges.

The police officer in charge of the investigation into his death, Glenn Browne, was the first witness to give evidence on Monday. In response to a question from O’Neil, he said he was surprised there wasn’t a warning that Deacon suffered from mental ill-health given his prior history.

“The purpose of warning is to convey the most important information to police when responding to incident,” he said.

He said he presumed there was an HIV warning because Deacon told an officer he was HIV positive during a prior arrest, despite it being a delusion.

During Judy Deacon’s questioning of Browne, she asked what he thought could be done to prevent people dying like her son.

“I’m not completely sure, Mrs Deacon, I wish things could be done better, I wish there were better ways,” Browne responded.

“The reality is they deal with thousands of different types of incidents every day in their work and it’s very difficult to train them up to a high standard in respect of everything they attend.”

He later said: “Where there is a risk to personal safety, I doubt we will ever reach a point where ambulance officers will attend instead of us, I doubt there will ever be funding for experts to be there and help guide us through those incidents.”

Ward told the court Deacon was stuck in a “cyclical pattern” that included periods of hospitalisation and then eventual improvement which would lead him to being discharged into the community with a community treatment order and support plans in place.

“But eventually there would be deterioration in his mental health and or increase in drug use where he reached a point of crisis which led to another period of containment or custody sometimes following episodes of violence,” Ward said.

Ward listed a number of incidents during which Deacon posed a risk to himself and assaulted other people, including strangers and medical staff. She said these facts weren’t being raised to engage in “victim blaming”, saying Deacon did “not cause his own death” but “we can’t understand the dreadful circumstances of Jesse’s death without confronting the difficulties he confronted in life”.

Judy was joined in court by a number of family members of other victims who have died during interactions with police. They included Lisa Topic, whose daughter Courtney was fatally shot by police while she was experiencing a severe episode of psychosis in 2015.

“I’m hoping with the way I intend to question people, which is not to lay blame … but to bring out things to help your honour to put forward recommendations that are not only adhered to but are followed up and sustained into the future,” Judy said.

The inquest continues.

australia.title: Derryn Hinch remembered as ‘journalistic James Bond’ – as it happened
australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast The use of AI in automated decision-making by govern...
australia.content:
What we learned today – Monday 20 July

That’s all for today – we’ll leave our live coverage there and thanks for following along.

Before we go, let’s recap the day’s top headlines:

  • Anthony Albanese said Pauline Hanson should not be talking the country down as she appeared at a string of conservative political events and holidays with billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart in Europe.

  • Independent Schools Australia, the peak body for private schools, launched a campaign today to increase government funding, targeting key Labor and teal seats across the country.

  • Lee Hanson, the daughter of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, said her mother’s comments about the White Australia policy have been “misinterpreted”.

  • One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce claimed Pauline Hanson’s party did not support the White Australia policy but backed the idea of “mass deportations”, including people seeking medical appointments after overstaying their visas.

  • The federal MP for Isaacs and former attorney general Mark Dreyfus has told the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion about the “breach of that sense of safety” experienced by Jewish Australians since 7 October.

  • Friends and family of the late Derryn Hinch have continued tributes at the state funeral service for the former journalist and senator in Melbourne today.

  • Mia Freedman’s son Luca Lavigne, 28, has been appointed CEO of her family-owned podcasting and media empire Mamamia.

  • A prominent academic and Palestine advocate Randa Abdel-Fattah who withdrew from last year’s Bendigo writers’ festival over a controversial code of conduct for speakers has launched legal action against the event’s hosts.

  • An LGBTQ+ inclusive arts space hosted inside a former Sydney church has been formally evicted by its landlords, according to the venue’s promoter, who described the move as feeling like “bigotry masquerading as moral victory”.

Thanks for joining us – see you again tomorrow morning.

Coles takes ACCC to court in bid to open second supermarket in Kalgoorlie

Coles has taken the competition watchdog to court in its bid to open another supermarket and liquor store in Kalgoorlie.

The supermarket giant is appealing in the federal court a decision by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC) to stop it from opening a second site in the West Australian mining hub.

The first case management or directions hearing in the matter will take place tomorrow morning in the federal court in Melbourne.

This type of hearing usually deals with administrative matters between the parties to determine a timeframe for providing further documentation and potential trial dates.

At the same time tomorrow, the federal court will hold a concurrent directions hearing relating to Coles separate appeal to the Australian Competition Tribunal against the ACCC’s decision.

The ACCC has determined another Coles in Kalgoorlie is likely to push out a smaller rival, reduce consumer choice and leave shoppers worse off.

Kalgoorlie has six supermarkets – two IGAs, a FoodWorks, Woolworths, Coles and Spudshed – and has previously had seven, including two Coles stores for much of the past decade.

What we learned today – Monday 20 July

That’s all for today – we’ll leave our live coverage there and thanks for following along.

  • Anthony Albanese said Pauline Hanson should not be talking the country down as she appeared at a string of conservative political events and holidays with billionaire benefactor Gina Rinehart in Europe.

  • Independent Schools Australia, the peak body for private schools, launched a campaign today to increase government funding, targeting key Labor and teal seats across the country.

  • Lee Hanson, the daughter of One Nation leader Pauline Hanson, said her mother’s comments about the White Australia policy have been “misinterpreted”.

  • One Nation MP Barnaby Joyce claimed Pauline Hanson’s party did not support the White Australia policy but backed the idea of “mass deportations”, including people seeking medical appointments after overstaying their visas.

  • The federal MP for Isaacs and former attorney general Mark Dreyfus has told the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion about the “breach of that sense of safety” experienced by Jewish Australians since 7 October.

  • Friends and family of the late Derryn Hinch have continued tributes at the state funeral service for the former journalist and senator in Melbourne today.

  • Mia Freedman’s son Luca Lavigne, 28, has been appointed CEO of her family-owned podcasting and media empire Mamamia.

  • A prominent academic and Palestine advocate Randa Abdel-Fattah who withdrew from last year’s Bendigo writers’ festival over a controversial code of conduct for speakers has launched legal action against the event’s hosts.

  • An LGBTQ+ inclusive arts space hosted inside a former Sydney church has been formally evicted by its landlords, according to the venue’s promoter, who described the move as feeling like “bigotry masquerading as moral victory”.

Thanks for joining us – see you again tomorrow morning.

Liberal MP rejects Tony Abbott’s claim that multiculturalism has failed

The Liberal MP Dan Tehan has rejected claims by the former prime minister and party president Tony Abbott that “multiculturalism in Australia has failed”.

In a video shared on X last week by former deputy prime minister John Anderson, Abbott targets Muslim communities and argues that “diversity is not our strength”.

Speaking to ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Tehan said:

Tony is a former prime minister and he has his views on various issues.

I have always said, and will continue to say … multiculturalism has thrived in Australia.

But one of the problems that we’ve got at the moment is that the Labor party, through walking away from the essence of Australia’s values and making sure that everyone who comes here and makes up the wonderful rich fabric of Australia, needs to also understand the values which are so crucial to who we are as a nation. And my view is that that’s where we’re failing.

‘It’s over’: Divine Playhouse evicted from former church after protests

Kat Wong

An LGBTQ+ inclusive arts space hosted inside a former Sydney church has been formally evicted by its landlords, according to the venue’s promoter, who described the move as feeling like “bigotry masquerading as moral victory”.

Less than two weeks after it opened, Divine Playhouse’s landlord had terminated the venue’s lease.

Divine Playhouse’s promoter and founder of Heaps Gay Events, Kat Dopper, said:

It’s over: our lease terminated, our artists cancelled, our venue being cleared out.”

That’s freedom of expression in Australia right now: some voices get amplified, others get evicted. In this case, it feels like bigotry masquerading as moral victory.

The pop-up was located in Sydney’s central business district inside a former church, which was deconsecrated in the 1930s and has spent most of the years since as a theatre.

Christian groups protested its opening night, claiming the venue’s organisers and performances were mocking religious faith, and pointing to social media images of drag queens dressed as nuns and a performer dressed as a pig offering French fries as holy communion.

Dopper vowed to continue fighting as she announced a “sing-in” protest, set to take place at 12pm on Saturday at Hyde Park.

If we walk away, they’ll believe that intimidation works and they’ll come back, again and again, for every other group they don’t agree with.

Divine will rise again.

Anne Aly rejects ‘competitive’ framing of government responses to Islamophobia and antisemitism

The multicultural affairs minister, Anne Aly, has called for an end to the “consistent comparison” between government responses to Islamophobia and antisemitism.

It comes after the secretary of the Lebanese Muslim Association questioned the difference between the government’s recent announcement on tackling Islamophobia and its full adoption of the antisemitism special envoy Jillian Segal’s report in December.

Speaking on ABC’s Afternoon Briefing, Aly said she takes “a bit of an issue” with the “consistent comparison”. She said:

Both are worthy of pursuit in their own right. Both the elimination of antisemitism and the elimination of Islamophobia and racism in all its forms are worthy pursuits, so I don’t want to get into a competitive kind of environment of Islamophobia v antisemitism, and I take issue with that.

Palestinian academic launches discrimination claim against writers’ festival organisers

A prominent academic and Palestine advocate who withdrew from last year’s Bendigo writers’ festival over a controversial code of conduct for speakers has launched legal action against the event’s hosts.

In a post to social media, Randa Abdel-Fattah announced she has filed a discrimination lawsuit against La Trobe University and Bendigo council on the grounds of political belief or activity. She said:

Universities and cultural institutions must be held accountable for their discrimination and anti-Palestinian racism.

Our fight against anti-Palestinian racism is only escalating. Efforts to silence our voices are expanding, with the goal of purging Palestinians and anti-Zionist voices.

The claim has been filed in the Victorian civil and administrative tribunal.

A spokesperson for the city of Bendigo declined to comment. La Trobe University has been contacted for comment.

This post was amended at 4.09pm. An earlier version incorrectly stated Abdel-Fattah had launched legal action against the organisers of Adelaide writers’ week.

‘A journalistic James Bond’: mourners continue tributes at Derryn Hinch’s state funeral

Derryn Hinch’s longtime friend and colleague Darren James led mourners through a state funeral for the former broadcaster and senator on Monday. James said:

He was a journalist, a newspaper reporter, a TV presenter, a godfather, an author, a senator and, a prisoner … he did it all.

Some people pass through life without leaving a ripple, he created tsunamis.

His ex-wife and friend, actor Jacki Weaver, sent a video tribute from America describing Hinch as a wonderful stepfather and companion. She also referenced Hinch’s reputation as a notorious ladies’ man, saying:

I’d like to pay my respects to all the women who loved Derryn, and who loved him back.

I won’t name them all … we don’t have time.

Former 3AW colleagues Denis O’Kane and Tony Tardio spoke of their love for Hinch, who was well known for his hatred of child sex offenders and those that shielded them. Tardio said:

There will never be another like him, even his name was unique.

He was a journalistic James Bond, drama followed him everywhere – even to his first wedding. And then he went on to marry three other times.

Australian woman who allegedly travelled to Syria to join Islamic State granted bail

An Australian woman accused of travelling to Islamic State-controlled Syria and being a member of the terror group has been granted bail, AAP reports.

Mother-of-four Rayann El Houli was charged in May with travelling to a declared conflict zone and joining IS.

The 34-year-old’s bid for bail was successful on Monday, with Melbourne magistrate Brett Sonnet accepting a combination of factors including the historical nature of her alleged offending and her role as primary caregiver.

He also took into account her compromised health including post-traumatic stress disorder and potential multiple sclerosis, a lack of prior offending and stable support in the community.

Sonnet also pointed to her living within the community for eight months without incident and her cooperation with authorities. The magistrate said on Monday:

In my view, the risk of reoffending is relatively low.

Stephanie Convery

That’s all from me today – I’ll hand you over now to my colleague Achol Arok who’ll take you through the rest of the afternoon.

One dead after Sunshine Coast blaze

A woman has died from her injuries after escaping a fire that gutted a Sunshine Coast apartment and prompted neighbours to evacuate, AAP reports.

The 21-year-old fled the blaze with another woman and was helped by neighbours before being taken to hospital.

She succumbed to her injuries, however, as police declared a crime scene at the Buderim site, with authorities yet to determine the cause of the fire.

Emergency services were called to the address at about 7:30pm on Sunday after reports one of the complex’s units was fully engulfed in flames. A 32-year-old woman was able to flee the fire uninjured, police said.

Residents of neighbouring units were evacuated as the fire engulfed the unit. Fire crews took about an hour to extinguish the blaze, police said.

An investigation into the blaze was in its early stages, Detective Senior Constable Robert Lowry told reporters in Maroochydore on Monday.

Penry Buckley

Jewish community security volunteer describes feeling of being ‘always on call’

The royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion has heard from another witness from the Victorian Community Security Group (CSG), appearing under the pseudonym ACR.

ACR, a CSG volunteer of almost 25 years who is involved in assisting national coordination, has described a feeling of being “always on call” following the escalation of antisemitic incidents since October 2023.

In emotional testimony, ACR has said they “very much discourage my family from attending Jewish community events”:

Particularly when I’m there in a CSG capacity, because selfishly I don’t want to put myself in a position where I would have to decide between extracting them or dealing with a threat if something arose, and so that’s that’s incredibly difficult. And then even when we do attend Jewish events from time to time when I’m there in a personal capacity as a member of a community, I’m never fully there is the reality, I’m always on alert.

ACR said by coincidence they were at Melbourne airport on the way to Sydney on the night of the Bondi terror attack in December:

I walked out of the airport and I drove straight to CSG headquarters, where I assisted with the operations and the crisis management that was occurring there, and remained there until the early hours the next morning.

Mia Freedman’s 28-year-old son to lead Mamamia

Amanda Meade

Mia Freedman’s son Luca Lavigne, 28, has been appointed CEO of her family-owned podcasting and media empire Mamamia.

Freedman and her husband, Jase Lavigne, co-founded the women’s digital media company in 2007 and now have the No 1 women’s podcast in Mamamia Out Loud.

Luca, who has been working in the business for a decade, most recently as chief operating officer and chief product officer, takes on the CEO role after Nat Harvey resigned to join Southern Cross Media Group as chief revenue officer.

Luca Lavigne said in a statement:

On behalf of the entire company, I wholeheartedly thank Nat for her outstanding leadership through a period of great opportunity and momentous change for the industry. Her leadership is defined by expertise, passion and dedication. This is a better business today because of her, and Nat will always have our friendship and our gratitude for everything she’s done during her time with Mamamia.

Guardian political reporter Josh Butler has wrapped together all the latest news on One Nation and party leader Pauline Hanson’s comments regarding “mass deportations” and the White Australia policy. Catch up on it here:

Pocock (not that one) challenges Farage in UK byelection

An Australian-born candidate has joined a record number of candidates challenging Nigel Farage in the byelection for the UK seat of Clacton.

A total of 34 candidates are standing, which is believed to be a record, according to Tendring District Council.

The list includes Daniel Pocock, a Swiss-Irish-Australian software engineer, born in the Melbourne suburb of Coburg. He gave an Australian address on the nomination form and is one of two foreign candidates (the other is from Belgium).

He will be running against candidates who include Baron von Thunderclap, Howling Laud Hope and Nick the Incredible Flying Brick (both from The Official Monster Raving Loony Party) and Woke Trump Carrzee – as well as, of course, the inestimable Lord Binface.

Penry Buckley

Jewish community security group requirements have doubled since 2023, royal commission hears

Jewish community security group protection requirements have doubled in the three years since the start of the conflict in Gaza, the royal commission on antisemitism and social cohesion has heard.

A volunteer for the Victorian Community Security Organisation (CSG), which like other CSGs in Australia, monitors threats to the Jewish community and provides security for schools, synagogues and events, has appeared under the pseudonym ACO at today’s hearing.

ACO, who holds a leadership role in the Victorian CSG, said national combined data showed the total number of volunteer hours had gone from 86,000 in 2024 calendar year to almost 114,000 hours in 2025.

Asked by counsel assisting, Tamara Philips, how much they estimated the total commitment per person across volunteer and paid members had increased since October 7, they said:

It’s fair to say that the requirements have nearly doubled in that period of time. Certainly, when it comes to the protection of events in our community; those numbers have doubled. When I look at the number of staff we have, that’s tripled.

When I look at the number of synagogues we’re protecting, that’s well over double the numbers that we used to protect. And whilst our volunteer numbers they do continue to grow, it’s nowhere near what we need in order to meet the operational requirements for our community.

More mourners arrive at Derryn Hinch’s state funeral

3AW presenter Denis Walter, the master of ceremonies for broadcaster Derryn Hinch’s state funeral, has arrived at the Timber Yard in Melbourne, as has 10 News journalist and presenter Jennifer Keyte.

South Australian electorate renamed after Lowitja O’Donoghue

Lowitja O’Donoghue, a trailblazing Aboriginal nurse turned Indigenous rights advocate, has been honoured with the renaming of a federal electorate, AAP reports.

The vast division of Grey, which covers the majority of South Australia, is being renamed as O’Donoghue, the Australian Electoral Commission announced on Monday.

O’Donoghue, a member of the Stolen Generations, was the first Aboriginal woman to be trained as a nurse and served as the founding chairperson of both the National Aboriginal Conference and the Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Commission. Her advocacy was pivotal to Australia’s native title legislation.

O’Donoghue was a Yankunytjatjara woman, with the electorate of Grey taking in most of the Anangu Pitjantjatjara Yankunytjatjara lands.

The AEC determined the name change despite 235 of the 310 community submissions arguing to retain Grey, named for Sir George Grey. The AEC found the arguments for change were “well detailed, informative, convincing and ultimately persuasive. This contrasted with most of the submissions objecting to the renaming of the electorate.”

The commission noted Sir George spent “a comparatively small part of his life” in Australia, with longer service to the British empire in South Africa and New Zealand, and the AEC decided “the time had come to recognise the outstanding contribution to Australia and its people made by a distinguished Australian”.

The decision comes after an AEC proposal last week to rename the southern Tasmanian seat of Franklin to Tongerlongeter, after an Indigenous warrior who fought colonisation, then took on a leadership role for Aboriginal Tasmanians exiled to Flinders Island.

The AEC has opened consultations on the Franklin switch, which comes after a radical re-drawing of the electorate’s boundaries.

australia.title: Afternoon Update: Spain claim World Cup glory; Derryn Hinch farewelled; and how John Carpenter learned to shock
australia.snippet: Want to get this in your inbox every weekday? Sign up for the Afternoon Update here , and start your day with our Morning Mail newsletter...
australia.content:
Good afternoon.

Spain defeated defending champions Argentina with a bruising 1-0 victory in extra time to hoist the Fifa World Cup for the first time since 2010.

Argentina and star player Lionel Messi showed flashes of promise, attempting to hold their ground with10 men after Enzo Fernández was sent off.

But Spain’s defence proved unassailable as substitute Ferran Torres scored in extra time to propel his team to victory.

The final’s controversial half-time show gave viewers an eclectic mix of ballads, football legends and the Muppets.

After the game, the US president, Donald Trump, and Fifa president, Gianni Infantino were booed before the US leader attempted to gatecrash Spain’s victory party.

Top news

  • Barnaby Joyce says One Nation doesn’t want return of White Australia policy but backs Pauline Hanson on mass deportations

  • Ban on protests outside synagogues and Jewish schools should be considered, Dreyfus tells royal commission

  • The Odyssey storms global box office with $264m opening

  • Australia spent more than $9m for each asylum seeker held on Nauru last year – so why can’t they afford to buy food?

  • Taxpayers could pay millions to abuse survivors if Christian Brothers goes bankrupt, court documents reveal

  • ‘When I get home, my whole body aches’: extreme heat saps health and wages of India’s poorest workers

In video

Vila Cururu, an illegal gold-mining settlement at the heart of Brazil’s most desecrated Indigenous territory, was a hive of depravity until just a few weeks ago. The Guardian has gone on the ground with the Brazilian forces fighting to eradicate illegal mining that has destroyed protected areas of Indigenous land.

What they said …

“He was a journalistic James Bond, drama followed him everywhere – even to his first wedding. And then he went on to marry three other times.” – Tony Tardio.

The former 3AW newsreader paid tribute to his ex-colleague Derryn Hinch at the former broadcaster and senator’s state funeral in Melbourne.

Podcast

World Cup Daily: Spain are world champions

Max Rushden, Barry Glendenning, John Brewin, Jonathan Wilson and Sid Lowe discuss Spain’s win at the 2026 World Cup, the issues that plagued Argentina, the showbiz and the epic third-place playoff.

Listen to the episode here

Before bed read

‘Everything I know about evil I learned in that small town’: John Carpenter on terrifying the world with Halloween, The Thing and The Fog

At 78, the king of horror and sci-fi movies is as much of a rebel as ever. He speaks with Steve Rose about his dreams, his nightmares and how he became addicted to moviemaking.

Daily word game

Today’s starter word is: ATT. You have five goes to get the longest word including the starter word. Play Wordiply.

Sign up

world.title: São Tomé and Príncipe heads to polls in tense presidential election
world.snippet: Incumbent Carlos Vila Nova hopes to defeat his former party and secure second term as independent Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to t...
world.content:
Voters in São Tomé and Príncipe go to the polls for a presidential election on Sunday as one of Africa’s least populous countries seeks to burnish its democratic credentials.

According to the National Election Commission, about 142,000 people are registered to vote in the tiny African state’s elections, approximately 15% of whom live in the diaspora.

Since gaining independence from Portugal in 1975, the island country off Africa’s west coast has built a solid reputation for peaceful, competitive elections. But this year’s vote comes amid a tense political atmosphere and a lingering constitutional crisis.

The president, Carlos Vila Nova, is running for a second term as an independent, rather than as the candidate for the ruling Acção Democrática Independente (ADI), whom he represented when he was elected in 2021.

The tensions between Vila Nova and his former party began in January last year when he dismissed the prime minister, Patrice Trovoada. Trovoada’s replacement, the former justice minister Ilza Amado Vaz, resigned after just three days, before the current holder, Américo Ramos, took office.

On Sunday, Vila Nova will be running against four other candidates including the ADI parliamentary leader, Nito D’Abreu. Another former prime minister, Jorge Bom Jesus, attempted to withdraw his independent candidacy, but missed the deadline and remains on the ballot.

The main opposition party, the Movement for the Liberation of São Tomé and Príncipe, is now part of a broad coalition backing the incumbent president, despite being staunch ADI opponents. Meanwhile, an ADI faction led by Ramos is backing D’Abreu. If no candidate receives more than 50% of the vote, the election will go on to a second round.

The businessman Domingos Monteiro, known as “Nino”, who has been president of the São Toméan Football Federation since 2015, was disqualified after the constitutional court ruled he did not meet the eligibility requirements. Monteiro was born on the island, but his parents never became naturalised citizens after moving from Cape Verde where they were born.

“The constitutional court is violating the principle of equal rights … It is time for descendants born in São Tomé and Príncipe to say no to discrimination, to the culture of xenophobia and persecution,” said Monteiro.

For voters, priorities include tackling government corruption, high inflation, severe youth unemployment, chronic fuel shortages, and frequent blackouts. Rivals of Vila Nova are hoping this will keep him from a second term and propel them to the presidency.

Corruption in São Tomé and Príncipe “is the greatest catastrophe the country has experienced in this half-century [of independence”, D’Abreu said at the presidential debate on Tuesday.

The country is seen as a trusted western ally for security and maritime trade in the Gulf of Guinea, one of the world’s biggest maritime piracy hotspots. It also has offshore oil deposits that make a significant contribution to its economy. Observer missions from the European Union, G7+ and the Community of Portuguese Language Countries are on the ground to monitor the polls.

world.title: ‘We are preserving a tradition’: how Ghana’s sensationalist film posters became collectible art
world.snippet: Hand-painted works are often wildly unfaithful to the movies they portray – reinterpretations that sometimes resulted in threats, insults...
world.content:
Sitting on his porch in Teshie near Accra, Heavy J dipped a brush into red oil paint and dabbed it carefully on to his canvas – a flour sack – adding blood to a knife being wielded by a man. Higher on the canvas, he had started on an outline of a skull.

Heavy J was creating a poster, but not as you might have expected for a horror film. Instead, it was for the animated fairytale The Little Mermaid. The man with the knife was not a killer but the film’s kind-hearted prince, Eric. The skull was also unrelated to the story. “We add more to make people interested,” said Heavy J, whose real name is Jeaurs Affutu.

Hand-painted film posters by local artists were a hallmark of Ghanaian film culture from the late 1970s to the early 2000s, used to advertise screenings for neighbourhood venues known as video clubs after organisers realised that the original posters were not attracting enough audiences.

Plot lines were regarded as little more than jump-off points for humorous and surreal flights of fancy. Artists working for different video clubs competed to make the best “forgery”, as they described their interpretations.

The practice began to wane around the turn of the century as more Ghanaians gained access to electricity and their own TV sets and video players. Many video clubs went out of business and painters pivoted to create other work. But by then the posters had attained global interest, popularised in books and foreign exhibitions, and old and rare paintings became prized collectibles.

There was a lull in interest in newly painted posters in the early part of the 21st century, but demand has risen, driven by online marketing and a receptive customer base of film lovers in the west.

Deadly Prey Gallery has been working with artists to preserve the culture of making hand-painted film posters, while helping meet the increased demand.

Named after an action film, the business was co-founded in 2012 by Brian Chankin, then a video rental store owner in Chicago, and Robert Kofi, a Ghanaian who, as a child, used to work as a “hype man” for video centres in his home town of Winneba and later started collecting and selling posters. They partnered after Kofi sold Chankin some works.

Deadly Prey Gallery works with 15 artists, including Heavy J, who has been painting posters for four decades, connecting them to online customers and shipping the artwork on completion.

Most orders come from the US. Old action, science fiction and horror films have the highest demand. Popular titles include The Exorcist and the Star Wars and Terminator franchises. And prices for commissioned pieces start at $600 (£450) and vary based on the canvas size and other customer preferences.

Kofi, who is based in Accra, is part manager and part editor. He identifies the artists most suited for each work, shares his vision of the posters with them and makes regular visits to their workspaces to review works in progress.

In a studio in Ashaiman, about 11 miles from Heavy J’s house, another artist called Stoger was working on two commissions: one for the horror film Poltergeist, and another for the experimental drama Gummo, which contains multiple acts of violence against cats and a scene in which a character eats spaghetti in a bath tub.

The poster showed three cats and a man in a bath with a plate of spaghetti in front of him. In his feedback that day, Kofi, speaking in Ga, a primary language of Ghana, told Stoger two of the cats were not aggressive enough and the food was too clean. “I want uglier cat scenes,” he later explained. “The spaghetti has to be dirtier.”

Stoger, born Benjamin Amartey, was a sculptor before developing an interest in films and becoming a poster painter in 1992. “I use my imagination to make scenes that will attract people so that they’ll love the poster,” he said.

The emphasis on exaggeration comes from an African tradition of “visualising the invisible”, said Joseph Oduro-Frimpong, the director of the Centre of African Popular Culture at Ashesi University and a poster collector himself.

“The posters’ audiences have not seen the film, so it’s impossible for them to know [whether they are accurate]. Therefore, the artists tap into what they call imaginative painting,” he said. “They will highlight these things and in doing so they incorporate things that are not in there. There is a kind of sensationalism to it.”

The reinterpretations at times resulted in threats, insults and even physical attacks from viewers who felt duped. Kofi laughed when he recalled an incident in the 1990s when people beat him up after they watched the action film Double Impact and realised it did not have a scene showing Jean-Claude Van Damme carrying out a beheading, as was illustrated on the poster.

At the Centre for National Culture in Accra, dozens of colourful posters from Deadly Prey Gallery are pinned on wooden walls. They include Jennifer Lopez launching an arrow at a snake in Anaconda, and a mouse coming out of Jamie Lee Curtis’ mouth in Halloween.

“We are preserving a tradition,” Kofi said of the poster-painting craft. “We are preserving a history.”

world.title: Seven Americans quarantining at Kenya Ebola facility after US travel ban, says aid group
world.snippet: Aid workers are first known people to quarantine at facility, which sparked huge opposition in Kenya Seven American aid workers who had b...
world.content:
Seven American aid workers who had been in Congo to fight the Ebola outbreak are quarantining at a new isolation facility in ⁠Kenya after the US government introduced travel ⁠restrictions, the head of a US charity ​employing them told Reuters.

The aid workers are the first known people to quarantine at the facility, which has sparked huge opposition in Kenya and is at the heart of a legal case in which a court has ordered the work to be ⁠suspended. Construction continued, however, according to US officials and satellite imagery reviewed by Reuters.

Washington’s new policy says American citizens returning from the Democratic Republic of the Congo, where there is an Ebola outbreak, must spend three weeks in a third country before entering the United States.

The US government is building ⁠the 50-bed bio-isolation unit on an air force base in central Kenya for asymptomatic Americans exposed to the virus in Democratic Republic of the Congo or Uganda. Many Kenyans are angered at what ​they see as the US offloading the health risk such patients pose.

Last month, Kenya’s ‌health minister announced an immediate halt to the facility’s ‌construction after he was found in contempt of court for failing to observe the order to halt work pending a final ruling.

“Samaritan’s Purse has seven American Disaster Assistance Response Team staff ‌members there,” Franklin Graham, president and CEO of Samaritan’s Purse, told Reuters in response to questions.

“None of them have any symptoms, but they are being quarantined by the Kenyan government for 21 days,” Graham said.

A US state department official told Reuters a group of asymptomatic Americans who had served on the frontlines of the Ebola response had “voluntarily moved to the Kenya facility for precautionary monitoring and isolation”.

“Kenyan authorities have authorized their movement into the facility under the observation of the US public health service clinicians,” the official said, adding that the decision was taken “strictly out of an abundance of caution”.

Kenyan health ministry officials did not immediately respond to calls or requests for comment ‌on the move. A senior Kenyan foreign ministry official said they had no information on it.

Another source familiar with the matter who asked for anonymity said that the group had arrived at the site in central Kenya on Monday and were sleeping in army cots in tents.

He said some ​had treated Ebola patients at the Christian aid group’s treatment centres in Congo but others had carried out work such as construction, with no direct contact with the sick.

“There is one potential high-risk exposure,” he said, adding that their health was being monitored. Kenyan authorities are not allowing the group to leave the facility to travel anywhere else in the country, he added.

The often fatal viral disease spreads through direct contact with bodily fluids from infected people or animals.

Samaritan’s Purse, which has been promised several million dollars from the Trump administration for the ⁠Ebola response, is an evangelical Christian group that works in disaster zones around the world.

It is one of the biggest foreign ​aid groups treating Ebola in Congo and has the largest number of ​Americans there, working closely alongside the World Health Organization to ​contain the outbreak. One of its US staff members who caught Ebola earlier this month was transferred to a hospital in Germany on Monday.

world.title: UK aid cuts ‘reduce bilateral support to some African countries by 90%’
world.snippet: Critics say Foreign Office figures send ‘global message about the role the country wants to play on international stage’ Labour’s foreign...
world.content:
Labour’s foreign aid cuts mean reductions of as much as 90% in the bilateral support the UK will give to some African countries, Foreign Office figures show.

The department’s annual report includes a long-awaited breakdown of how the reduction in the aid budget will affect individual countries for the next three years.

Analysis by Bond, the umbrella group for development charities, shows cuts of 90% for Mozambique and Malawi by 2029, 80% for Rwanda and Sierra Leone and 49% for Somalia.

Bond’s chief executive, Romilly Greenhill, said: “By slashing UK aid funding to countries like Ethiopia, Malawi, Mozambique, Rwanda, Sierra Leone and Uganda, this Labour government is abandoning communities on the frontlines of conflict and the climate crisis and risks plunging these countries’ populations into poverty and instability.”

Keir Starmer’s government announced deep reductions to spending on overseas aid last year to fund increases in the defence budget, prompting the resignation of Anneliese Dodds as development minister.

Part of Labour’s approach in implementing the cuts has been to switch its focus to funding multilateral donors such as the World Bank, which it argues is a more efficient use of straitened resources.

Explaining the cuts in a written statement to parliament in March, the foreign secretary, Yvette Cooper, said: “In a range of countries, we will transition away from spending high levels of grant ODA [overseas development assistance], but our ambition and effort will remain high – delivering through modernised partnerships, and making the most of what the UK has to offer.”

Charities, however, say the scale of the reduction in direct support to individual countries will jeopardise vital projects.

The director of global outcomes at Save the Children, Lisa Wise, said: “Today’s international budget allocations reflect what we already know – reductions in public investment in countries and children that need it most. These choices send a global message about the role the UK wants to play on the international stage.”

The next steps for Labour’s development policy will fall to the incoming prime minister Andy Burnham’s pick for foreign secretary. The current energy secretary, Ed Miliband, is seen as a likely contender for the role.

Some MPs have urged Burnham to act to restore the party’s leadership on development, including by setting a path back towards the target of spending 0.7% of national income on overseas aid.

The UK takes on the chair of the G20 next year – the coordinating body that includes China, India and Brazil alongside wealthy countries in the global north.

Greenhill urged the new PM and foreign secretary to use that role “to champion the global reforms needed to address poverty and inequality among the world’s marginalised communities”.

The development minister, Jenny Chapman, said: “The world has changed. Crises in one part of the world now affect us all.

“Just this year, conflict in the Middle East has driven up food and fertiliser costs and the Ebola outbreak that began in the DRC is an urgent reminder why global health security matters.

“We’re not turning away from these challenges. We’re making every pound of UK development spending work harder, for people facing the toughest crises and for taxpayers at home.”

world.title: Uganda calls for travel restrictions to be lifted after last Ebola patient discharged
world.snippet: Country begins 42-day countdown to outbreak being declared officially over, as numbers continue to rise in neighbouring Democratic Republ...
world.content:
Uganda has started lobbying countries to lift Ebola-related travel restrictions after discharging its last confirmed Ebola patient from hospital.

The discharge of a Congolese national from the Mulago national referral hospital’s isolation centre in Kampala on Thursday triggered the start of a 42-day countdown required by the World Health Organization before Uganda can officially be declared Ebola-free, provided no new infections are detected.

The outbreak in the country infected 20 people and claimed two lives.

Fifteen countries continue to maintain either partial or full travel restrictions on Uganda after the outbreak, measures the government said have crippled tourism, trade and business, despite the country’s relatively successful response.

The US has placed Uganda on a level four advisory against all travel due to the Ebola outbreak. The same category includes countries such as North Korea, Somalia, Afghanistan and Russia.

“As we make progress in managing this disease, we are engaging and asking those countries with a view to opening up so that the economy does not get injured,” Uganda’s health minister, Dr Chris Baryomunsi, said after the ceremony marking the release of the last patient.

Baryomunsi said the country was not yet Ebola-free – under WHO guidelines, countries must complete two consecutive 21-day incubation periods without recording a new case before an outbreak can officially be declared over.

“This is an imported outbreak. We remain on high alert because what we are celebrating here is different from what is happening in the Democratic Republic of the Congo,” he said.

The DRC reported ⁠on Thursday that ⁠the ​number ‌of ‌confirmed ‌cases in the country had ‌risen to ​2,073, including ⁠796 ​deaths, as ​of ​14 July. The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo strain of the virus, was first declared by the WHO on 17 May.

Uganda’s outbreak has been markedly different from previous Ebola emergencies in the region, with only two deaths and 20 confirmed infections including 15 Congolese nationals, four health workers and one driver.

WHO’s representative in Uganda, Dr Kasonde Mwinga, said the country’s response demonstrated the value of sustained investment in epidemic preparedness.

“The case fatality rate of less than 10% is among the lowest recorded in Ebola outbreaks because the lowest has always been 30%. That is not by luck. It is because people invested in preparedness,” she said.

Mwinga said Uganda had established treatment facilities, trained emergency medical teams and pre-positioned medical supplies before the outbreak, allowing authorities to respond rapidly when cases were detected.

The outbreak also accelerated scientific efforts to develop vaccines against the Bundibugyo strain of Ebola, for which no licensed vaccine exists.

Dr Ronnie Bahatungire, the clinical services commissioner at Uganda’s health ministry, said the country had already participated in trials involving experimental therapies during the outbreak and plans to join vaccine studies. “We will participate at whatever point in time when an opportunity arises,” Bahatungire said.

This week, Oxford University’s Oxford Vaccine Group launched the world’s first Phase I clinical trial of BD-Ebov, a vaccine candidate targeting the Bundibugyo strain, in response to the outbreak, with the first patient already enrolled.

Despite Uganda’s progress, authorities said the threat remains across the border. Baryomunsi said presidents Yoweri Museveni of Uganda and Félix Tshisekedi of DRC had agreed on closer cross-border cooperation and signed a bilateral memorandum of understanding, where Uganda has already sent health experts to DRC to contain the outbreak and stop Congolese travelling to Uganda to seek medical attention.

“We have so far sent 50 health workers with four laboratories and these have been set up in four different locations. We agreed that if they require additional human resources, we shall send more depending on how the situation progresses,” Baryomunsi said.
